### The Thermal Signature in Wiper Control Circuits

Your observation that warmer temperatures resolve the intermittent failure and abnormal speed is the critical diagnostic clue here. In automotive electrical systems, components that behave erratically under load but function correctly when thermal dissipation increases are almost exclusively pointing toward a failing power transistor or an intermittent connection within the control module's internal circuitry. The 2004 Dodge Ram 1500 utilizes a wiper motor assembly that integrates a three-speed relay and a Park Switch, often referred to as the WIPER MOTOR CONTROL MODULE (WCM), located directly behind the right-side cowl panel near the firewall.

When you activate the high-speed setting, the circuit demands significantly higher current than low or intermittent speeds. If the internal contacts of the WCM are corroded, pitted, or if the solder joints on the integrated circuitry have fatigued due to repeated thermal cycling, the resistance in that path increases. As ambient temperature drops and the engine bay cools overnight, this compromised connection creates enough voltage drop to cause erratic behavior. The "super fast" wiping you observed is likely a symptom of the control logic failing to latch the low-speed relay, causing high current to bypass intended regulation and drive the motor at maximum RPM regardless of the stalk position.

Troubleshooting should begin by isolating whether the fault lies in the module or the wiring harness feeding it. While replacing the entire wiper motor assembly is a common repair for this era of Ram, it is often unnecessary if the issue is strictly electrical at the control head. You can perform a voltage drop test using a multimeter while an assistant operates the wiper stalk. Connect one probe to the power feed wire (typically black/yellow or similar depending on specific trim) and the other directly to the battery terminal positive post. If you see more than 0.5 volts of drop under load, suspect high resistance in the wiring harness connectors leading to the cowl area. These connectors are notorious for developing green corrosion that expands when cold, breaking contact momentarily before warming up restores conductivity.

Another potential culprit is the Park Switch integrated into the motor assembly. This switch mechanically disengages the power once the wiper arms reach their resting position to prevent battery drain. If this internal switch is failing due to age or debris accumulation, it can create a feedback loop where the control module misinterprets the arm position, leading to erratic speed modulation or the motors stopping mid-stroke until the circuit resets via a power cycle at the stalk.

If you decide to replace the unit, verify that the new assembly matches your specific application year and engine configuration (5.7L Hemi), as harness variations exist between Quad Cab and Regular Cab models. Before committing to parts replacement, ensure the ground strap for the wiper motor is clean and tight; a poor ground can mimic many of these symptoms by creating an unstable reference voltage for the control logic.

### Systematic Diagnosis Steps

1.  **Inspect Cowl Connectors**: Remove the right cowl panel (under the hood near the windshield base). Check the plastic connectors leading to the wiper motor for corrosion or loose pins. Clean and reseat them.
2.  **Voltage Drop Testing**: With the ignition on and wipers running, measure voltage drop across the main power feed and ground connections. Values exceeding 0.5V indicate bad wiring or corroded terminals.
3.  **Module Swap Test**: If connectors are sound, swap the WCM with a known good unit if available, or replace it as a last resort before investigating deeper harness issues.

The thermal dependency you identified strongly suggests internal component degradation within the control module itself rather than a simple fuse issue. Fuses protect against short circuits; they do not degrade in resistance over time to cause variable speeds unless physically damaged. The solution often lies in addressing the thermal expansion and contraction cycle that stresses the solder joints inside the WCM, leading to the exact symptoms you are experiencing.
